hints: Look at what each particle can offer, does $PH_3$ have a lone pair and does $H^+$ have any electrons at all?
Remember phosphorus in $PH_3$ has only three bonds, so it still holds one lone pair ready to be shared.
Think about what we call a covalent bond when both shared electrons come from just one atom, and what new ion this makes.
walkthrough:
**Draw out what PH3 looks like**

Phosphorus is in Group 15, so it has 5 outer electrons. In $PH_3$ it uses three for bonding to hydrogen and keeps two as a lone pair.

Structure idea:
$$PH_3 \text{ has a lone pair on P} + H^+ \text{ has no electrons}$$

**See what H+ needs**

A hydrogen ion, $H^+$, is just a proton. It has an empty 1s orbital and really wants a pair of electrons to get a stable duplet.

Reaction idea:
$$PH_3 + H^+ \rightarrow PH_4^+$$

**Name the new bond**

The lone pair on P is donated into the empty orbital on $H^+$. Both electrons in the new P-H bond come from phosphorus.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{shared pair from one atom = dative covalent (coordinate) bond}$$

**Check the product**

This gives the phosphonium ion, $PH_4^+$, exactly like $NH_3 + H^+ \rightarrow NH_4^+$. It is a strong covalent bond, not just a weak intermolecular force.

options.A: Correct. The lone pair on phosphorus in $PH_3$ is donated to the empty orbital of $H^+$ to form $PH_4^+$. Because both electrons are supplied by phosphorus, this is a dative covalent (coordinate) bond.
options.B: Not correct. Dipole-dipole forces are weak intermolecular forces between permanent dipoles in separate neutral molecules. Here a new strong chemical bond is formed to make $PH_4^+$.
options.C: Not correct. A hydrogen bond needs H attached to highly electronegative N, O or F interacting with a lone pair on another molecule. Phosphorus is not electronegative enough, and $H^+$ forms a full covalent bond, not a partial hydrogen bond.
options.D: Not correct. An ionic bond needs complete transfer of electrons to form oppositely charged ions that attract. Here electrons are shared (even though both come from P), so the P-H bond in $PH_4^+$ is covalent, not ionic.
